Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled "A Neuronal Role for SNX6 in Dendritic Trafficking of the Postsynaptic Scaffold Protein Homer1b/c" for consideration at eLife. The new version of your manuscript was reviewed by the Editor and one of the previous reviewers and, once again, they are not satisfied with the limited revisions you have made in response to their criticisms. Their initial reaction was to reject your paper with no chance for reconsideration but I requested they give you one last chance and here is their firmly written opinion that you simply must take seriously if you wish to have this work published in eLife:

Specifically, in the previous decision letters we have very clearly indicated that we cannot offer to publish your paper in the current form, because the reviewers found that your major claim that " SNX6 mediates long-range vesicular transport of Homer1b/c to distal dendrites" is not sufficiently supported by data. With other words, it is possible that SNX6 indeed mediates long-range transport of Homer1b/c, but it is also possible that Homer1b/c arrives to the dendritic spines by diffusion alone, and the interactions that you described serve another function (if any). Given the complexity of the subject and the large amount of work that you have put into revising this manuscript, we have offered you an opportunity to completely and thoroughly revise the whole paper in a way that would make it clear to the reader from the start to the end that your transport-related conclusions are not more than one of the possible explanations of the mouse phenotypes that you nicely describe. Such re-writing would entail not a minor but a major revision of your paper. Given your new suggestion for the title and the minor edits you have done, it is very clear to us that you are not willing to perform such a major revision. We of course fully respect your decision, because this is your paper, and you should write it in the way you find most appropriate. We would like to emphasize that your English writing is perfectly fine, and that our negative decision is only due to the fact the reviewers were not convinced that your major conclusion is sufficiently supported by data. We would also like to emphasize that since the reviewers are not co-authors of your paper, it is not their task to search for "sentences or words in the manuscript still misleading or overstated" – it is up to authors to make such changes.

We are willing to give you one more chance to re-write the paper. However, you would need to really thoroughly rethink and revise the whole manuscript to provide a more balanced view of different ways in which their data can be explained. You are very much in favor of pushing through the model that SNX6 mediates transport of Homer1b/c on vesicles, but the experimental support for this model is insufficient and the FRAP data directly contradict it. Therefore, the paper needs to be re-written in a way that would make it clear to the reader that transport of Homer1b/c on endosomes is not more than one of the possible explanations of the observed mouse phenotypes. Trying to solve the problem by adding a few disclaimers here and there is not enough, and also not what we have asked for. For example, in the latest version, you proposed to revert to the title with transport being the main message, while we asked for this change one revision before.

results.result: CNS-specific Snx6 knockout mice exhibit deficits in spatial learning and memory, as demonstrated by impaired performance in the Morris water maze test. The behavioral phenotypes suggest that ablation of SNX6 affects synaptic function of hippocampal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C22, C23, and C24 provide converging behavioral evidence from Morris water maze tests showing deficits in spatial learning, memory, and recall in CNS-Snx6 KO mice (Figure 2J-M). Claim C25 provides established knowledge about hippocampal function in spatial memory, and C26 draws a reasonable inference connecting the behavioral phenotypes to hippocampal synaptic function. The behavioral data are well-documented with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

results.result: Ablation of SNX6 causes a specific decrease in spine density in the distal apical dendrites of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, without affecting spine morphology or CA3 neurons. This indicates that SNX6 is required for spine morphogenesis and/or maintenance in CA1 distal apical dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 provide consistent morphological evidence from confocal microscopy (Figure 3C-D) and TEM (Figure 3G-H) showing decreased spine density specifically in CA1 distal apical dendrites but not in CA3 neurons. The specificity of the phenotype (CA1 vs CA3, spine density vs morphology) strengthens the conclusion in C31. The quantitative analysis appears rigorous with appropriate sample sizes.

results.result: SNX6 directly interacts with Homer1b/c through its N-terminal PX domain binding to the coiled-coil domain of Homer1b/c. This interaction is specific to Homer1b/c (not Homer1a, Homer2b, or Homer3) and occurs on early endosomes in dendrites.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary approaches support this interaction: mass spectrometry (C37, Figure 4C), in vitro binding assays (C38-C40, Figure 4D-G), co-IP in cells and brain lysates (C41-C42, Figure 4H-I), immunoisolation (C43-C44, Figure 4I), and colocalization studies including superresolution microscopy (C45-C47, Figure 4J-N). The specificity for Homer1b/c over other Homer isoforms and family members is well-demonstrated. The convergence of multiple independent methods provides strong support.

results.result: Ablation of SNX6 causes reduced distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites, with decreased puncta number in dendritic segments and reduced fluorescence intensity in spines. This phenotype is rescued by overexpression of SNX6, demonstrating that SNX6 is required for Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 provide quantitative immunofluorescence data (Figure 5A-F) showing decreased Homer1b/c in distal dendrites and spines of Snx6-/- neurons, with accumulation in the soma. The rescue by SNX6 overexpression (C51) provides strong evidence for specificity. Notably, PSD95 distribution is unaffected (C52), indicating specificity of the phenotype. The conclusion in C54 is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The decreased spine density in Snx6-/- neurons can be rescued by overexpression of SNX6 or full-length Homer1c, but not by a Homer1c fragment lacking the EVH1 domain. This indicates that SNX6-dependent dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c contributes to spine formation/stabilization through Homer1b/c's scaffolding function.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 provide rescue experiment data (Figure 5G-H) showing that both SNX6 and full-length Homer1c restore spine density, but Homer1c-C (lacking EVH1 domain) does not. This structure-function relationship supports the inferences in C57-C58 that Homer1b/c's scaffolding function is required. The rescue experiments provide strong evidence for the mechanistic link between SNX6, Homer1b/c distribution, and spine maintenance.

results.result: A small fraction (~10%) of Homer1c puncta are motile in dendrites, moving bidirectionally on SNX6-positive vesicles with mean velocity of 0.416 μm/s. These motile puncta are predominantly small (<0.3 μm²), consistent with vesicular structures. Ablation of SNX6 dramatically reduces the fraction of motile Homer1c puncta.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C66 provide live imaging data (Figure 6A-C, Videos 2-4) with quantitative analysis of Homer1c mobility. The size distribution analysis (C61, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) supports the vesicular nature of motile structures (C62). The dramatic decrease in motile puncta in Snx6-/- neurons (C66) provides strong evidence for SNX6's role in Homer1c transport. The specificity is demonstrated by lack of comovement with GluN1 (C65).

results.result: SNX6 mediates dynein-dynactin-driven transport of Homer1b/c in dendritic shaft. Superresolution microscopy shows colocalization of SNX6, Homer1b/c, and dynein-dynactin components on vesicles. Inhibition of dynein activity or disruption of SNX6-dynactin interaction reduces Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 provide multiple lines of evidence: superresolution microscopy (C67, Figure 6D), pharmacological inhibition with Ciliobrevin D (C68, Figure 6E-H), dominant-negative p150Glued-N (C69, Figure 6I-J), immunoisolation (C71, Figure 6K), and colocalization analysis (C72, Figure 6L-M). The convergence of these approaches strongly supports the conclusion in C73 that SNX6 mediates dynein-dynactin-driven transport of Homer1b/c.

results.result: Homer1b/c trafficking is distinct from PSD95 trafficking and does not rely on the secretory pathway. Live imaging shows no colocalization of SNX6/Homer1b/c with motile PSD95 clusters, and PKD-KD expression (which blocks secretory trafficking) does not affect Homer1b/c distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 provide live imaging with retrospective staining (Figure 7A, Video 12) showing that motile PSD95 clusters lack SNX6/Homer1b/c. Claims C76-C77 show that blocking secretory trafficking with PKD-KD does not affect Homer1b/c distribution (Figure 7B-E). These negative results are important for defining the trafficking pathway and are well-controlled.

results.result: Homer1b/c translocates from dendritic shaft to spines by protein diffusion, which does not require SNX6 or vesicular transport. Live imaging rarely detects Homer1c puncta entering spines, spine:shaft ratios remain constant in Snx6-/- neurons, and FRAP analysis shows similar recovery kinetics in wild-type and Snx6-/- neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 provide live imaging evidence (Figure 8A, Videos 13-14) and spine:shaft ratio analysis (Figure 8B) showing that SNX6 is not required for Homer1b/c entry into spines. Claims C82-C85 provide FRAP data (Figure 8C-D) showing similar recovery kinetics in wild-type and Snx6-/- neurons, supporting diffusion-based entry. The conclusions in C86-C87 are well-supported by the convergence of live imaging and FRAP data. The FRAP results are consistent with prior literature (Kuriu et al., 2006).

results.result: Ablation of SNX6 causes impaired AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission and decreased surface levels of AMPAR (GluA1 and GluA2), without affecting NMDAR-mediated transmission or surface GluN2B levels. The impairment is postsynaptic, not presynaptic.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 provide electrophysiological evidence (Figure 9B-D) showing ~50% reduction in AMPAR eEPSCs with no change in NMDAR eEPSCs or paired-pulse ratio, indicating a postsynaptic mechanism. Claims C91-C92 provide surface staining and biotinylation data (Figure 9E-K) confirming decreased surface AMPAR but not NMDAR. The rescue by SNX6 or Homer1c overexpression (C92) supports specificity. The convergence of electrophysiology and biochemistry provides strong support.

results.result: Dendritic loss of Homer1b/c caused by SNX6 ablation leads to increased mGluR5 surface expression and increased AMPAR endocytosis. Inhibition of mGluRs rescues AMPAR surface expression in Snx6-/- neurons, indicating that the AMPAR phenotype is mediated by dysregulated mGluR signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 provide evidence for increased mGluR5 surface levels (Figure 9K, Figure 9—figure supplements 2-3) and increased AMPAR endocytosis (Figure 9L-M) in Snx6-/- neurons. Claim C95 shows that mGluR inhibition rescues AMPAR surface expression (Figure 9N-Q), providing strong mechanistic evidence. The conclusion in C96 is well-supported by the pharmacological rescue experiment, which establishes a causal link between mGluR dysregulation and AMPAR phenotype.

results.result: SNX6 functions independently of retromer to regulate Homer1b/c distribution in dendritic shaft. VPS35 depletion produces distinct phenotypes from SNX6 ablation, and live imaging shows no comovement of Homer1c and VPS35-labeled vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 show that VPS35 depletion causes different phenotypes than SNX6 ablation (Figure 10C-H), with decreased Homer1b/c throughout the cell but no change in spine distribution or mGluR5 levels. Claims C102-C104 provide live imaging (Figure 10I-J, Videos 15-16) and colocalization data (Figure 10—figure supplement 2) showing minimal interaction between Homer1b/c and VPS35 pathways. The conclusion in C105 is well-supported by the distinct phenotypes and lack of colocalization.

results.result: Ablation of SNX6 causes uncoupling of the endocytic zone (EZ) from the postsynaptic density (PSD), with a ~2-fold increase in clathrin-negative synapses. This may contribute to lower AMPAR surface levels in dendritic spines.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 provides immunostaining data (Figure 9—figure supplement 4) showing increased fraction of clathrin-negative synapses in Snx6-/- neurons. The inference in C98 that this contributes to AMPAR phenotype is reasonable given the known role of EZ-PSD coupling in AMPAR trafficking (Lu et al., 2007). However, this is a correlative observation and the causal contribution is not directly tested.

results.result: SNX6 is a ubiquitously expressed PX-BAR protein that is expressed in mouse brain neurons, primarily in dendrites, with partial colocalization with the postsynaptic marker PSD95 but not the presynaptic marker synaptophysin.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 states established knowledge about SNX6 function. Claims C10-C13 provide expression and localization data from Western blots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), immunohistochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E), and quantitative analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H). The data support the expression pattern and subcellular localization described.

results.result: CNS-Snx6 KO mice are viable with normal brain size and structure, and show no deficits in locomotor activity, mood-related behaviors, sociability, social novelty, repetitive behaviors, or performance in Y maze and shuttle box tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C20 provide observational and behavioral data (Figure 1E-F, Figure 2A-G) showing that CNS-Snx6 KO mice are grossly normal in many behavioral domains. Claim C21 shows normal performance in Y maze and shuttle box (Figure 2H-I). These negative results are important for establishing the specificity of the spatial learning and memory deficits. The behavioral battery is comprehensive.

results.result: SNX6 colocalizes primarily with early endosome markers (EEA1, Rab5B) and partially with late endosome marker Rab7, Rab4, and TGN46, but not with Golgin97 or Rab11. This suggests SNX6 associates with endosomes and transport carriers in dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 provide colocalization data (Figure 4A-B) showing the subcellular distribution of SNX6 on various vesicular compartments. The inference in C36 is reasonable based on the colocalization pattern. The data establish the endosomal localization of SNX6 in dendrites, which is important context for understanding its function.

results.result: Summary of main findings: Ablation of SNX6 in the CNS causes deficits in spatial learning and memory, decreased spine density in CA1 distal apical dendrites, impaired AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission, and decreased Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites. These phenotypes can be rescued by overexpressing Homer1b/c or SNX6.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C111 are summary statements of the main findings from the study. They accurately reflect the data presented in the manuscript and the conclusions drawn from multiple lines of evidence. These claims synthesize the major results into a coherent narrative about SNX6's physiological function in CNS excitatory neurons.
